claims.claim: Features are the measurable properties of an example that a model uses as inputs; in a house-price model the features include size, number of rooms, and location.
A feature, also called a dimension, is an input variable used to generate model predictions.
The label is the known answer attached to an example; in a house-price model the label is the price the house sold for.
A supervised training example couples feature values with a known label value; training data includes both, and the model uses them to predict unknown labels for future cases.
Feature quality sets the ceiling on model quality: high-quality data improves model performance, while poor or noisy data leads to inaccurate predictions.
Choosing and preparing features is human work: feature engineering selects the most relevant aspects of raw data for the task, is context-dependent, and requires domain knowledge.
Labeled datasets are data points together with their correct outputs, sometimes called ground truth, and labeling data takes a lot of time and effort.
Unsupervised learning learns from data without labels, while supervised learning requires labeled examples; the presence or absence of labels is the boundary between them.
Dimensionality reduction reduces the number of features in a dataset, illustrating that features are numerous, human-chosen inputs rather than fixed facts.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources differ in what they call a feature (input variable, dimension, predictor, attribute), and some explainers blur the line between feature selection and feature extraction.
positions: IBM treats 'feature' and 'dimension' as synonyms and notes many sources use feature engineering and feature extraction interchangeably
Google Cloud consistently uses 'features' for the inputs of a supervised model
Microsoft Learn uses 'feature values' paired with 'label values'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the widely shared definition, features are the inputs a model looks at, with IBM's input-variable framing as the technical anchor; selection-versus-extraction distinctions belong to a practitioner course and are not taught here.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the features-versus-labels distinction belongs inside supervised learning or stands as its own topic.
positions: The supervised-learning sibling lesson introduces features and labels briefly and points readers to this lesson
This lesson owns the full treatment, including feature quality and the human work of choosing features
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson teaches the distinction in depth while keeping the supervised learning loop, classification, and regression inside the sibling topic, per the curriculum's topic ownership.
